New York Police Arrest 23 In "Drug Sweep" Of Washington Square
"Mostly For Possession and Sale Of Marijuana"

The UPI has reported that New York City police arrested 23 people Friday in a "drug sweep" of Washington Square Park at the edge of Greenwich Village and in the heart of the New York University campus. Police say the arrests were mostly for possession and sale of marijuana.

One of the costs of prohibition is the problem of contraband sales in public parks. This is certainly not a desirable situation for people who want their children to have a place to play. I have been offered marijuana myself when I walked through Washington Square. Naturally, I was just amused, but I can understand that some people might be offended.

Mayor Giuliani is taking credit for a drop in violent crime in the city. However, the drop is nationwide and shows little correlation to greatly differing police practices. Unfortunately, he has also made a crack down on marijuana a major goal of his administration. Several perverse consequences are easily predictable.

First, there will be an increase in violence, because sales in places as public as parks tend to inhibit violence.

Second, there will be an increase in hard drug dealing, because marijuana is more easily suppressed as a factor of its relative bulk, and dealers in private will be less inhibited about carrying an inventory of other substances.

Third, organized crime will become more involved as the result of the need for more elaborate facilities. Anyone can sell in a park, but only someone with operating capital can own a "store."

Fourth, there will be an increase in police corruption as result of the involvement of organized crime.

Fifth, all of these costs of prohibition will naturally be blamed on marijuana, and the cycle will either accelerate or the police will be distracted and the contraband business will simply move back the parks. Déjà vu all over again, as a much nicer New Yorker once said.

New York needs a new LaGuardia Commission, and the city that was once called New Amsterdam needs to learn from the successes of the city that gave birth to it.

Richard Cowan
